matchApplication: This assessment combines the advanced pressure and contest behaviours required throughout Australian football. It measures whether players can create turnovers through coordinated tackling, ground-ball pressure, influenced disposals, controlled spoiling and repeat defensive effort while preserving the wider team structure.
relatedDrills: TD-050 – Defensive Pressure and Contest Assessment

title: Defensive Reset After Opposition Switch Mark
Team Defence Structure and Adaptability Assessment
Final-Ninety-Seconds Boundary Defence
primarySkill: Managing boundary-side defence and stoppages during the final stages of a close match.
objective: Develop players’ ability to use the boundary, control stoppages and make disciplined defensive decisions during the final 90 seconds of a close match.
groundSize: One boundary-side half of the ground from the centre wing to the goal line.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Set the defending team five points ahead with 90 seconds remaining.
Begin with the opposition in possession near the boundary at half-forward.
Position players for a likely boundary contest or stoppage.
Nominate a score-and-time communicator.
Establish the applicable stoppage and boundary restart rules for the playing group.
Run repeated scenarios from marks, throw-ins, ground balls and free kicks.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to score before time expires.
The defence protects the inside route and directs possession towards the boundary.
At boundary stoppages, defenders protect the corridor-side exit.
If the defence wins possession, players decide whether to retain, advance along the boundary or take a safe mark.
If the football leaves the area, the coach restarts with the appropriate scenario and adjusts the clock.
Deliberate illegal time wasting results in a turnover or free kick to the attack.
The attacking team receives an immediate repeat entry after a rushed central defensive turnover.
The repetition ends when time expires, the score changes or the defence establishes secure possession.
coachingPoints: Know the score and remaining time.
Protect the corridor side of every boundary contest.
Use the boundary without relying on illegal or reckless actions.
Maintain one defender behind the immediate contest.
Prevent the attacking team from releasing backwards into central space.
Communicate stoppage roles before the restart.
After winning possession, select a legal low-risk option.
Avoid taking the football into unnecessary central congestion.
Remain prepared for the opposition to switch quickly.
Do not concede avoidable free kicks through undisciplined contact.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players understand the match situation.
Whether the inside stoppage exit is protected.
Whether a deeper balance player remains.
Whether the defence uses the boundary intelligently.
Whether possession decisions suit the clock.
Whether the team remains alert to a switch.
Whether the defence avoids unnecessary free kicks.

commonErrors.error: Defenders attack from the boundary side and open the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Position inside and force possession towards the line.

commonErrors.error: Every defender enters the stoppage.
commonErrors.correction: Retain inside cover and one deeper balance player.

commonErrors.error: Players attempt illegal time wasting.
commonErrors.correction: Use lawful possession, marks and boundary movement.

commonErrors.error: A defensive win is kicked blindly into central space.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the football and choose a controlled boundary or support option.

commonErrors.error: Defenders become unaware of a switch.
commonErrors.correction: Keep weak-side communication and scan beyond the immediate contest.

progressions: Reduce the lead to one point.
Start from a defensive free kick near the boundary.
Give the attacking team an extra player.
Begin after the opposition scores a behind and the defence must take a kick-in.
regressions: Allow defensive organisation before each restart.
Pause after possession changes to discuss the decision.
successIndicators: Protect the inside route at boundary contests.
Use the boundary legally and effectively.
Prevent a high-value central scoring opportunity.
preserve the lead until time expires.
matchApplication: The final stages of close matches demand precise tactical and legal decision making. Boundary control, stoppage organisation and possession security can prevent the opposition from gaining the central access required for a winning score.

title: Defensive Wing Fold and Corridor Screen
primarySkill: Using the defensive-side wing to fold behind possession and protect the corridor.
objective: Develop the defensive wing’s ability to narrow behind the football, screen central movement, support long contests and expand again when possession changes sides.
groundSize: Two-thirds of the ground using the full width.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position the attacking team with possession on one wing.
Arrange defenders across forward, midfield and backline units.
Nominate one defender on the opposite wing as the defensive folding wing.
Place attacking gates through the corridor and both wings.
Establish a likely long-kick contest on the ball side.
Place two defensive rebound gates on the opposite side.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attack moves possession along one side of the ground.
The defensive-side wing narrows behind the football into a corridor-screening position.
If the attack kicks long down the line, the wing folds behind the contest to provide cover or ground-level support.
If the attack switches, the wing expands towards the new receiver while another teammate assumes the central screen.
The wing communicates runners entering from behind.
Defenders score one point for denying the corridor, two points for winning the long contest and three points for rebounding through the opposite gate.
The attack scores three points for a clean corridor break.
Rotate wing and midfield roles after each block.
coachingPoints: The defensive wing should narrow when the football is on the opposite side.
Protect the corridor without becoming so narrow that the wide switch is uncontested.
Move before the ball carrier disposes.
Fold behind the expected long contest rather than arriving level with it.
Identify forwards and midfielders running into central space.
Communicate who replaces the corridor-screening position when expanding.
Retain goal-side movement during switches.
Support the first defensive possession after the turnover.
Expand quickly after possession is secured.
Avoid standing stationary between opponents without affecting a passing lane.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the wing narrows early enough.
Whether the corridor passing lane is genuinely affected.
Whether the wing reaches the back of long contests.
Whether the far-side switch remains defendable.
Whether the wing supports the defensive rebound.

commonErrors.error: Defensive wing remains on the boundary away from play.
commonErrors.correction: Narrow into a central screening position behind the football.

commonErrors.error: Wing moves directly towards the contest and arrives in front.
commonErrors.correction: Fold around the back to provide goal-side cover.

commonErrors.error: The switch is completed before the wing reacts.
commonErrors.correction: Read the ball carrier’s preparation and expand while the kick travels.

commonErrors.error: No teammate replaces the central screen.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate the rotation before moving towards the new ball side.

commonErrors.error: Wing wins possession but disposes without support.
commonErrors.correction: Connect with the nearest midfield or half-back outlet.

progressions: Add a second long contest after the initial rebound.
regressions: Mark the folding wing’s reference position.
Allow the coach to call fold and expand movements.
successIndicators: Support the back of long contests.
Expand in time to pressure switches.
Connect with teammates after the defensive win.
matchApplication: The wing away from the football plays an important defensive role by protecting the corridor, supporting contests and preventing the opposition from moving directly through the centre. The role changes quickly when possession switches sides.
relatedDrills: TD-005 – Ball-Side Pressure and Weak-Side Cover

title: Half-Back Intercept-to-Outlet Unit
primarySkill: Connecting half-back intercept positioning with a reliable first outlet.
objective: Develop a half-back unit that influences the forward entry, wins possession and immediately connects with a safe supporting outlet.
groundSize: From the centre square to the goal line.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Arrange three to five half-back defenders across the top and inside defensive 50.
Position attackers across half-forward and inside 50.
Place one defensive midfielder in front of the half-back line.
Position two outlet players towards the wings.
Mark one central and two wide outlet gates.
Begin each repetition with the attack controlling possession across half-forward.
howTheDrillWorks:
The midfield defender pressures or screens the forward-entry options.
Half-backs adjust depth according to the pressure on the ball carrier.
One defender attacks the likely entry while teammates protect underneath and behind.
If the defence intercepts or wins the spill, the nearest outlet players create width.
The interceptor selects a short release, wide switch or controlled central connection.
The remaining half-backs retain turnover protection behind the first outlet.
Defenders score two points for the intercept and an additional point for a successful supported outlet.
The attack receives a repeat entry if the first outlet turns over.
coachingPoints: Entry pressure and intercept positioning must work together.
The interceptor should hold enough depth to attack the football moving forward.
Supporting half-backs protect short and ground-level options.
Outlet players must move as possession is being won.
The interceptor should scan before completing the mark or collection.
Avoid every defender spreading ahead of the football.
Use a short outlet when it removes pressure.
Use width when the corridor is congested.
Central rebound should be selected only when support and field position make it safe.
Rebuild defensive shape immediately after an unsuccessful outlet.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether entry pressure influences the attacking disposal.
Whether intercept defenders position at useful depth.
Whether teammates protect underneath the intercept.
Whether outlets move before possession is secured.
Whether the first disposal suits the pressure.
Whether the unit resets after a failed rebound.

commonErrors.error: Half-back stands directly beside the forward.
commonErrors.correction: Create intercept separation while maintaining opponent awareness.

commonErrors.error: Outlet players wait until the intercept is completed.
commonErrors.correction: Move during the flight of the entry kick.

commonErrors.error: Every defender runs forward after possession is won.
commonErrors.correction: Retain at least one player behind the rebound.

commonErrors.error: Interceptor immediately kicks long under little pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Use the free short outlet to secure the transition.

commonErrors.error: Failed outlet leaves the backline disorganised.
commonErrors.correction: Recover goal-side and rebuild line connection immediately.

progressions: Allow the attack to switch before entering.
Add a second forward entry after a failed outlet.
Require the rebound to progress into a forward entry.
Introduce scoreboard scenarios affecting the outlet decision.
successIndicators: Influence and read the forward entry.
Position to intercept moving towards the football.
Select a first disposal appropriate to the pressure.
Reset quickly after an unsuccessful exit.
matchApplication: Half-backs are not only responsible for winning intercept possession. The quality of the first outlet determines whether the defensive win becomes a controlled transition or another opposition entry.

title: Midfield Stoppage Sweep and Cover
primarySkill: Positioning a defensive midfielder behind a stoppage to protect the opposition’s forward exit.
objective: Develop the defensive sweep role behind stoppages so the midfield can pressure the first possession, protect the forward release and connect with the backline.
groundSize: Centre-square or midfield stoppage area measuring approximately 45 metres × 40 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Establish a central stoppage with ruck and midfield players.
Place three attacking exit gates forward, left and right.
Nominate one defender as the midfield sweep player behind the stoppage.
Position a half-back defender deeper as the next protective layer.
The attacking team may win possession through the front, side or back of the stoppage.
Rotate sweep, inside-midfield and half-back roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins with a ball-up, throw-in simulation or ground-ball stoppage.
Inside defenders pressure the first possession.
The sweep player positions goal-side of the likely forward exit.
If the football leaves through the front of the stoppage, the sweep player pressures, tackles or intercepts.
If possession exits laterally, the sweep player adjusts while maintaining central protection.
The deeper defender communicates runners moving beyond the sweep.
After winning possession, the defence connects through a rebound gate.
The defence scores for stopping the forward exit, recovering the spill and completing the first connection.
coachingPoints: The sweep player must begin goal-side of the stoppage.
Position close enough to affect the first clean exit but not so close that congestion removes vision.
Read ruck positioning and the body shape of inside midfielders.
Protect the forward and corridor-side release first.
Communicate with the deeper half-back line.
Do not become drawn into every ground-ball contest.
If the first exit is lateral, adjust without surrendering the centre.
Attack loose footballs moving forward.
After the turnover, provide or use the first safe midfield connection.
Rotate the sweep role when the stoppage moves.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the sweep player starts goal-side.
Whether the first forward exit is pressured.
Whether the player remains outside unnecessary congestion.
Whether lateral movement opens the corridor.
Whether communication connects midfield and half-back.
Whether the sweep player attacks loose possession.
Whether the first rebound disposal is supported.

commonErrors.error: Sweep player stands level with the stoppage.
commonErrors.correction: Begin behind the contest and protect the forward exit.

commonErrors.error: Player becomes trapped inside congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Hold enough separation to scan and close the release.

commonErrors.error: Lateral possession draws the sweep away from the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust while maintaining central protection.

commonErrors.error: No communication occurs with half-backs.
commonErrors.correction: Identify runners and the next layer before the stoppage begins.

commonErrors.error: Sweep player wins possession and kicks blindly.
commonErrors.correction: Connect with the nearest available support option.

progressions: Add an attacking midfielder beginning behind the sweep.
Move the stoppage to the wing and half-forward.
Add a second stoppage immediately after the first possession.
Continue a defensive regain into full-ground transition.
regressions: Pause after the first possession to assess positioning.
successIndicators: Protect the opposition’s forward stoppage exit.
Remain connected to the half-back line.
Pressure, intercept or recover the first release.
Connect effectively after the defensive win.
matchApplication: A defensive midfielder positioned behind the stoppage can prevent one clean clearance from exposing the backline. The role requires disciplined spacing, scanning and connection rather than simply joining the initial contest.

title: High-Forward Exit Denial Rotation
primarySkill: Rotating high forwards between ball pressure, short-outlet denial and long-contest coverage.
objective: Develop a coordinated high-forward unit that adjusts its responsibilities as the opposition changes between short exits, switches and long kicks.
groundSize: From the opposition goal line to the centre square.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position the opposition to begin from a kick-in or defensive possession.
Arrange three to five high forwards across the first defensive line.
Position midfield support behind the forwards.
Mark one central and two wide opposition exit gates.
Identify three rotating high-forward roles:
Ball-pressure player
Short-outlet defender
Long-contest support
Rotate players through each role.
howTheDrillWorks:
The opposition begins its exit from defensive 50.
The nearest high forward applies pressure to the ball carrier.
The second high forward protects the most dangerous short outlet.
The third forward positions to affect the likely long kick or second possession.
When the ball moves, the forwards rotate into new pressure, outlet and contest roles.
Midfielders compress behind the high-forward line.
The pressing team scores for forcing a hurried long kick, creating a turnover or regaining possession inside 50.
The opposition scores for an uncontested corridor exit.
coachingPoints: High forwards must defend as a unit rather than chase individually.
The ball-pressure player closes from the corridor side where possible.
The short-outlet defender arrives as the receiver takes possession.
The long-contest player must position before the kick is released.
Rotate roles immediately after each disposal.
Maintain connection with the midfield screen.
Do not allow all forwards to become trapped near the ball.
Recognise when the opposition has broken the first line and recover centrally.
After a regain, create width and scoring support.
Maintain legal pressure around marks and kick-ins.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether all three high-forward roles are occupied.
Whether short receivers are closed as possession arrives.
Whether the long kick is anticipated.
Whether roles rotate after each disposal.
Whether several forwards chase the same possession.
Whether players recover after the first line is broken.

commonErrors.error: Every forward pressures the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Retain separate short-outlet and long-contest responsibilities.

commonErrors.error: The short receiver is allowed to turn.
commonErrors.correction: Close while the football is travelling.

commonErrors.error: Long-contest coverage reacts after the kick.
commonErrors.correction: Position before the ball carrier completes the disposal.

commonErrors.error: Midfield remains too deep behind the press.
commonErrors.correction: Compress towards the expected second possession.

commonErrors.error: High forwards stop after being bypassed.
commonErrors.correction: Recover through the corridor and reconnect with midfield.

progressions: Add scoreboard scenarios requiring higher or lower defensive risk.
Continue the regain into a complete scoring phase.
regressions: Use one side of the ground.
Allow the forwards to set before each restart.
successIndicators: Fill the pressure, outlet and long-contest roles.
Influence or contest the long kick.
Recover when the first defensive line is broken.
Convert regains into organised attacking opportunities.
matchApplication: High forwards begin the team’s defensive structure. Their ability to rotate between pressure, short-outlet denial and long-contest support determines whether the opposition exits cleanly or is forced into predictable possession.
relatedDrills: TD-063 – Forward-Line Press with Behind-Ball Cover

title: Wet-Weather Territory Defence
primarySkill: Defending territory and ground-level possession under wet-weather conditions.
objective: Develop a defensive method suited to wet conditions in which players protect central territory, expect imperfect possession and prevent dangerous ground-level exits.
groundSize: Two-thirds of the ground, with selected boundary-side contest zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Use damp footballs to simulate reduced handling reliability without deliberately creating an unsafe surface.
Mark central high-risk territory and two wider low-risk channels.
Position teams in realistic structures.
Establish several ground-ball and aerial-contest starting points.
Place territorial target zones near the boundary and away from goal.
Check footing and reduce contact intensity if the surface becomes unsafe.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins with an aerial kick, bouncing football or contested ground ball.
The attacking team attempts to move centrally and score.
Defenders protect the corridor and force possession towards wider territory.
Around loose footballs, the nearest player pressures while teammates protect the release.
Aerial defenders spoil towards the boundary or support rather than back towards goal.
If defenders cannot secure clean possession, they may knock or kick the football towards a territorial target zone.
Defenders score for forcing the football wide, creating a stoppage in safe territory or completing a controlled exit.
The attack receives bonus points for clean central possession after a defensive handling error.
coachingPoints: Expect the football to spill and position for the second possession.
Protect central territory before attempting low-percentage possession.
Use the boundary as a defensive support.
Stay on the feet around ground-ball contests where practical.
Avoid unnecessary short handballs in heavy congestion.
Spoil and knock the football towards safe territory.
Maintain one player outside congestion for the release or next spill.
Communicate the safest direction before the contest.
Secure possession with body protection when a clean gather is available.
Adjust contact and speed to the safety of the conditions.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players anticipate handling errors and spills.
Whether all defenders collapse into congestion.
Whether aerial spoils move away from goal.
Whether disposal choices suit the conditions.
Whether players maintain safe balance and contact.
Whether the team accepts stoppages in favourable territory.

commonErrors.error: Defenders attempt difficult clean gathers in heavy congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Knock the football towards support or safer territory when possession is unlikely.

commonErrors.error: Players use repeated short handballs around a slippery contest.
commonErrors.correction: Use a direct territorial disposal or create a stoppage.

commonErrors.error: Spoils return towards the corridor or goal.
commonErrors.correction: Direct the football towards the boundary or defensive support.

commonErrors.error: Every defender enters the ground-ball contest.
commonErrors.correction: Retain release-lane and outside-balance players.

commonErrors.error: Intensity remains unchanged on an unsafe surface.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce contact and movement speed or relocate the drill.

progressions: Add match-like contact where conditions are safe.
Use scoreboard scenarios requiring territory protection.
Continue a defensive win into a controlled transition.
Allow the attack to deliberately create ground-ball chaos.
regressions: Pause between phases to restore organisation.
successIndicators: Force the football towards the boundary.
Create stoppages or turnovers in favourable areas.
Maintain technique and safety under wet conditions.
matchApplication: Wet-weather football increases spills, rushed disposals and repeat contests. Effective defence becomes more territorial, with strong central protection, boundary use and disciplined numbers around ground-level possession.

title: Four-Phase Team Defence Match Rehearsal
primarySkill: Maintaining the team defensive game plan through four consecutive match phases.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to move between major defensive phases without losing structure, communication or tactical clarity.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Arrange both teams in full positional structures.
Establish four consecutive phases:
Opposition kick-in
Midfield stoppage
Turnover transition
Repeat inside-50 entry
Nominate defensive leaders in each unit.
The coach controls restarts but provides no tactical instruction during play.
Set a scoreboard and time situation appropriate to the playing group.
Assign assistant coaches to observe separate defensive units.
howTheDrillWorks:
Phase One: The opposition begins with a kick-in and attempts to exit defensive 50.
When the phase ends, the coach immediately starts Phase Two from a midfield stoppage.
After the stoppage possession is resolved, the coach creates Phase Three through an unpredictable turnover.
The teams transition at full speed and play until a forward entry or defensive stop occurs.
The coach then introduces Phase Four as an immediate repeat entry against the defending team.
The defence must reorganise between phases without a huddle or coach instruction.
A successful defensive stop must be followed by an exit suited to the score and pressure.
Complete four to six full sequences before changing the scoreboard or tactical condition.
coachingPoints: Carry defensive communication from one phase into the next.
Defend kick-in possession beyond the first disposal.
Establish pressure, cover and balance around the stoppage.
React immediately when possession changes.
Protect the corridor during open transition.
Reassign opponents rather than searching for original match-ups.
Reset shape immediately after unsuccessful exits.
Maintain pressure and ground-level organisation during repeat entries.
Adjust risk according to score and time.
Retain turnover protection after defensive wins.
Leaders should organise while players are moving.
Complete every phase rather than mentally resetting early.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether kick-in defence protects the second possession.
Whether the midfield stoppage has clear pressure and sweep roles.
Whether the corridor is protected during transition.
Whether defensive lines reconnect before the repeat entry.
Whether ground-level and aerial contest roles are organised.
Whether player leaders communicate between phases.
Whether defensive exits suit the match situation.

commonErrors.error: Players treat each phase as a separate drill.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain continuous communication and role awareness between restarts.

commonErrors.error: Kick-in defence relaxes after the first possession.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the planned second and third exit options.

commonErrors.error: Players react slowly to the turnover phase.
commonErrors.correction: Change direction immediately and protect the corridor.

commonErrors.error: Defenders search for original opponents during the repeat entry.
commonErrors.correction: Cover the nearest dangerous attacker and communicate new responsibility.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue causes several players to chase the same possession.
commonErrors.correction: Restore pressure, cover and balance roles.

commonErrors.error: Defensive wins are followed by unsuitable risk.
commonErrors.correction: Match the first exit to pressure, score and available support.

progressions: Remove advance notice of the phase order.
Change scoreboard information during the sequence.
Allow the attacking team to select its kick-in and stoppage methods.
Continue all regains into complete attacking phases.
regressions: Rehearse two phases at a time.
Allow 10 seconds for defensive organisation between phases.
Announce each phase before the restart.
Permit one short player huddle per sequence.
successIndicators: Maintain defensive connection through all four phases.
Defend kick-ins and stoppages with clear roles.
Win possession and make an appropriate transition decision.
matchApplication: Matches move rapidly between set plays, turnovers, open transition and repeat entries. This rehearsal tests whether the team’s defensive game plan remains stable when those phases occur consecutively without coaching pauses.

title: Team Defence Chapter Final Assessment
primarySkill: Applying the complete team-defence system in unrestricted match conditions.
objective: Assess whether the team can independently establish, maintain and adapt a complete defensive system across all major Australian football phases and match situations.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Arrange both teams in full match structures.
Nominate defensive leaders, but require all players to communicate local information.
Prepare a balanced assessment sequence containing:
Slow opposition possession
Fast centre-square launch
Opposition kick-in
Forward-half press
Long down-the-line contest
Full-width switch
Outnumbered defensive transition
Repeat inside-50 entries
Boundary stoppage
Late-game lead protection
Immediate possession-regain requirement
Opposition-specific attacking pattern
Assign coaches to assess forward, midfield, backline and full-team behaviours.
Use a scoring rubric for structure, communication, pressure, contest work, adaptability and transition.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins each scenario without prescribing the required defensive solution.
The attacking team attempts to exploit the starting condition using unrestricted football.
The defence identifies the problem, selects a system and organises responsibilities.
Play continues through disposals, contests, turnovers and transitions until a score, controlled exit or natural stoppage occurs.
Tactical conditions may change during a repetition.
After a defensive win, the team must select an exit or attacking transition appropriate to the scoreboard and pressure.
Failed exits result in immediate repeat entries.
Coaches record outcomes without interrupting normal play.
Players complete a brief self-assessment between major blocks.
The final phase is an uninterrupted match-simulation block in which the defence must operate without coach instruction.
coachingPoints: Establish connected defensive shape before applying unnecessary pressure.
Maintain goal-side positioning and protect high-value central space.
Coordinate pressure, cover and balance around possession.
Adjust defensive depth according to pressure on the football.
Communicate opponent handovers and movement between lines.
Protect the corridor while maintaining weak-side coverage.
Use pressing triggers collectively.
Delay correctly when outnumbered.
Organise aerial, ground-level and stoppage contests.
Create intercept opportunities through influenced disposals.
Reset immediately after unsuccessful exits and repeat entries.
Select between direct accountability, zone, press and delay according to the situation.
Adjust risk to scoreboard and time.
Retain turnover protection after winning possession.
Use player leadership to organise the system.
Maintain legal technique and structural discipline under fatigue.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: The speed and accuracy of initial defensive organisation.
Connection between forward, midfield and backline units.
Pressure, cover and balance around the football.
Defensive depth relative to ball pressure.
Repeat defensive efforts and reset speed.
Quality of the first possession after a defensive win.
Consistency under fatigue and repeated phases.

commonErrors.error: Players chase the football without maintaining team shape.
commonErrors.correction: Re-establish connected lines and dangerous-space protection before escalating pressure.

commonErrors.error: Defensive depth does not reflect pressure on the kicker.
commonErrors.correction: Compress when pressure is strong and protect behind when pressure is absent.

commonErrors.error: Multiple defenders perform the same role.
commonErrors.correction: Clearly identify pressure, cover, balance and deeper protection.

commonErrors.error: Runners become free between defensive lines.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate and confirm handovers before responsibility is released.

commonErrors.error: Aggressive pressure has no protection behind it.
commonErrors.correction: Retain a deeper balance layer or reduce the risk of the press.

commonErrors.error: The team fails to reset after an unsuccessful exit.
commonErrors.correction: Recover goal-side immediately and rebuild the structure for the repeat entry.

commonErrors.error: Players use the same defensive system in every scenario.
commonErrors.correction: Select the response according to pressure, numbers, field position, score and time.

commonErrors.error: Defensive regains are followed by rushed disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession, scan and connect with the safest effective support option.

commonErrors.error: Communication decreases under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Require early names, locations and action calls throughout every phase.

commonErrors.error: Players wait for coach instruction.
commonErrors.correction: Empower leaders and nearby players to identify and call the required solution.

progressions: Remove all advance notice of scenarios.
Allow the attacking team to choose how it attempts to break the defensive system.
Change score, time and player numbers during live play.
Require players to review video and grade their own defensive performance.
Assess the team against a different opposition game plan in the next session.
regressions: Assess one defensive phase at a time.
Limit the defence to two available systems.
Allow brief organisation periods before restarts.
Use assistant coaches to guide separate defensive units.
successIndicators: Protect the corridor and central scoring areas.
Maintain goal-side, weak-side and behind-ball protection.
Recognise when to press, delay, match or zone.
Defend aerial, ground-level and stoppage contests.
Recover after broken lines and failed exits.
Adjust defensive risk to score and time.
Maintain legal technique and communication under fatigue.
Win possession and complete a supported transition.
Operate effectively without continuous coach direction.
matchApplication: This final assessment integrates the complete Team Defence chapter. It measures whether players can organise a full-ground defensive system, adapt it to changing match conditions, win possession and transition without sacrificing the structure required if the football turns over again.
relatedDrills: TD-040 – Defensive Movement Under Fatigue Assessment
TD-060 – Advanced Pressure and Contest Assessment
TD-080 – Team Defence Structure and Adaptability Assessment
TD-090 – Advanced Tactical Team Defence Assessment
TD-099 – Four-Phase Team Defence Match Rehearsal

title: Turnover Recognition Reset
objective: Develop players’ ability to immediately recognise whether their team has gained or lost possession and adopt the correct attacking or defensive position without waiting for further instruction.
groundSize: 30 metres long × 25 metres wide, divided into one central possession area and four outside positioning gates.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Mark a central 20-metre × 20-metre possession area.
Place two wide attacking gates outside the left and right edges of the area.
Place two narrow defensive gates closer to the corridor.
Divide players into two evenly numbered teams.
One team begins with the football while the other team shadows without applying contact.
The coach stands outside the area with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The team in possession moves the football by kick or handball inside the central area.
Players without possession maintain light shadow pressure but cannot intercept initially.
The coach calls “turnover” and either gives the football to the other team or rolls a new football into the area.
Players must immediately call either “ours” or “theirs” according to the new possession state.
The team gaining possession spreads towards the two wide attacking gates.
The team losing possession compresses towards the two central defensive gates.
Players hold their new structure for three seconds before play resumes.
After several repetitions, allow defenders to intercept naturally so the turnover cue becomes less predictable.
Rotate the starting team after each one-minute block.
coachingPoints: Players must identify possession change before beginning their movement.
Encourage loud, early communication from more than one player.
The team gaining possession should create width and depth rather than crowding the football.
The team losing possession should protect the corridor before chasing outside.
Players nearest the football should respond differently from players positioned further away.
Avoid all players reacting directly towards the football.
Players should scan before the turnover so their first movement is informed.
Reinforce immediate role change without disappointment, hesitation or argument.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players recognise the change of possession immediately.
Whether attacking players create usable width and depth.
Whether defensive players compress towards dangerous central space.
Whether players continue performing their previous role after possession changes.
Whether the nearest players and furthest players adopt appropriate different responses.

commonErrors.error: Players continue moving as though their team still has possession.
commonErrors.correction: Stop the repetition and require players to call “ours” or “theirs” before moving.

commonErrors.error: Every player runs directly towards the football.
commonErrors.correction: Assign outside players responsibility for width and inside players responsibility for corridor protection.

commonErrors.error: Players react only after the coach gives a second instruction.
commonErrors.correction: Remove the second instruction and reward the first team that reorganises independently.

commonErrors.error: Communication comes after the movement has already started.
commonErrors.correction: Require the possession call to be made immediately when the football changes teams.

commonErrors.error: Players walk into their transition positions.
commonErrors.correction: Set a three-second movement target while keeping the drill non-contact.

progressions: Allow defenders to intercept passes naturally rather than relying on the coach’s turnover call.
Add a three-second scoring bonus when the attacking team reaches a wide gate quickly.
Add a central scoring gate that the defending team must protect.
Increase the number of players and enlarge the area.
Allow full live play for 15-second periods after each turnover.
regressions: Use only four players per team.
Walk players through the attacking and defensive shapes before beginning.
Use a whistle and clear visual signal for each possession change.
Remove the football and practise the movements as a recognition exercise.
Give each player a fixed attacking and defensive starting position.
successIndicators: Change direction within one second of the turnover.
Protect central space before chasing wide.
Perform the transition response without waiting for the coach.
matchApplication: Australian football regularly changes from attack to defence or defence to attack without a stoppage. Players who recognise the turnover quickly can create an immediate numerical advantage, close dangerous space, provide an outlet or prevent the opposition from using the corridor.

title: Attack-to-Defence Recovery
primarySkill: Recovering defensively after losing possession in attack.
objective: Develop the ability to recover from an attacking position into an organised defensive shape immediately after possession is lost.
groundSize: 50 metres long × 35 metres wide with an attacking scoring zone, a central recovery line and a counterattack scoring gate.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark an attacking scoring zone at one end of the area.
Mark a counterattack gate at the opposite end.
Place a recovery line approximately 15 metres behind the attacking scoring zone.
Divide players into an attacking team and a defending team.
Begin with the attacking team positioned ahead of the recovery line.
Position the defending team compactly near the scoring zone.
The coach stands near the attacking end with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession and attempts to enter the scoring zone.
The defending team applies controlled pressure and attempts to intercept or win the football.
When the defending team gains possession, it immediately counterattacks towards the opposite scoring gate.
The player nearest the turnover applies pressure to delay the counterattack.
Other former attacking players sprint goal-side and recover through or towards the central recovery line.
Recovering players must protect the corridor before defending wider options.
The counterattacking team scores two points for reaching the opposite gate and one point for carrying or disposing through the recovery line.
The recovering team scores one point for forcing the football wide and two points for regaining possession before the opposition reaches the gate.
Reset after a score, turnover, boundary exit or 30 seconds of play.
Swap attacking and defending roles after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: The nearest player should pressure and delay rather than attempting an unrealistic immediate tackle.
Players further from the football must recover goal-side at speed.
Recovery runs should be directed towards dangerous space, not simply towards an opponent.
Protect the corridor before defending lower-risk boundary space.
Players should communicate who is pressuring, covering and protecting the deepest option.
Defenders must avoid running past the ball carrier and opening a central lane.
Once the counterattack is slowed, the defensive group should balance and match opponents.
Transition running should continue until the defence is organised, not only until players cross the recovery line.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the nearest player delays the counterattack.
The direction and speed of recovery runs.
Whether recovering players identify the most dangerous opponent.
Whether communication establishes clear defensive roles.
Whether players stop running once they reach the recovery line.
Whether the team can convert frantic recovery into an organised defensive shape.

commonErrors.error: Players chase the football from behind.
commonErrors.correction: Direct off-ball players to recover goal-side and protect the corridor.

commonErrors.error: The nearest player dives in and is evaded.
commonErrors.correction: Coach the player to close space under control and delay the disposal.

commonErrors.error: Recovering players run towards wide opponents first.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise central space and the deepest dangerous option.

commonErrors.error: Players jog after losing possession.
commonErrors.correction: Score transition effort and rotate players who repeatedly fail to recover.

commonErrors.error: Defenders recover to the same line with no depth.
commonErrors.correction: Establish pressure, cover and deeper balance roles.

progressions: Add an extra counterattacking player to create numerical disadvantage.
Begin the attacking team deeper inside the scoring zone.
Allow the counterattacking team only eight seconds to score.
Require the recovering team to win possession and immediately counterattack back.
Increase the field width to create more difficult defensive decisions.
regressions: Give the recovering team a numerical advantage.
Require the counterattacking team to complete one sideways disposal before advancing.
Use touch pressure rather than tackling.
Reduce the required recovery distance for Over 35 players or returning players.
successIndicators: Protect the corridor before wide space.
Communicate dangerous opponents and open space.
Prevent direct, uncontested counterattack through the centre.
matchApplication: When a team turns the football over during an attacking phase, many players may be positioned ahead of the ball. Effective attack-to-defence transition requires immediate pressure and purposeful recovery to prevent the opposition from counterattacking through an exposed corridor.

title: Boundary Contest Rebound
primarySkill: Rebounding from a contested possession near the boundary.
objective: Develop the ability to secure a boundary-side contest and transition into open space without forcing a high-risk central disposal.
groundSize: 40 metres long × 30 metres wide with a narrow boundary contest lane and two exit gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a five-metre-wide contest lane along one boundary.
Place a safe boundary exit gate ahead of the contest.
Place a higher-value central release gate on the opposite side of the area.
Divide players into two teams.
Position three to five players from each team near the contest lane.
Position outside support players through the central and far-side space.
The coach begins each repetition with a ground ball, high ball or pressured pass into the boundary lane.
howTheDrillWorks:
Both teams contest for the football inside the boundary lane.
The team gaining possession must establish control before selecting an exit.
A nearby teammate provides a safe down-the-line option.
Central and far-side players provide release options away from the boundary.
The boundary gate scores one point.
The central release gate scores three points but may only be used when the receiver has clear separation.
A central turnover gives the opposition three points.
The team losing possession applies immediate pressure and attempts to trap the football near the boundary.
Play continues until an exit, turnover, stoppage or 30-second limit.
Alternate the starting boundary after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Secure possession before attempting to move away from the boundary.
The safe down-the-line option should remain available.
Central release should be used only when the lane is genuinely clear.
Support players must not all enter the boundary congestion.
The ball winner should protect the football from boundary-side pressure.
Players behind the football should provide a reset.
The defending team should use the boundary as an extra defender.
Far-side players must remain engaged as potential switch options.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the ball winner protects possession.
Whether safe and aggressive exits are both available.
Whether defenders trap the football against the boundary.
Whether the team can later access central space after securing possession.

commonErrors.error: Players attempt an immediate blind disposal into the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the football and confirm the central receiver is clear.

commonErrors.error: All teammates crowd the boundary contest.
commonErrors.correction: Keep outside players in release positions.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier steps over the boundary unnecessarily.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the football while maintaining awareness of the line.

commonErrors.error: Players ignore the safe down-the-line option.
commonErrors.correction: Retain a boundary outlet when the centre is closed.

commonErrors.error: Defenders allow an easy inside release.
commonErrors.correction: Pressure from the corridor side and force play towards the line.

progressions: Require a switch after a successful boundary exit.
Add a recovering defender in central space.
Continue into a full-ground transition phase.
regressions: Give the ball-winning team an extra outside player.
Stop briefly after possession is secured.
Reduce contact for younger or returning players.
successIndicators: Secure contested possession near the boundary.
Use central space only when clearly available.
Escape the boundary pressure with retained possession.
matchApplication: Boundary contests reduce space and often attract numbers. Teams must secure the football, maintain a safe outlet and recognise when central space is genuinely available rather than forcing a dangerous release.

title: Corridor Break and Hold Width
primarySkill: Breaking through the corridor while preserving outside width.
objective: Develop a central transition that attacks through the corridor without drawing every supporting player into the same lane.
groundSize: 75 metres long × 55 metres wide with a central corridor and two outside support lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central corridor approximately 15 metres wide.
Mark one outside support lane on each side.
Place a scoring gate at the attacking end.
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Begin the transitioning team with possession near the defensive end.
Position defenders to pressure the corridor progressively.
Require at least one attacking player to remain in each outside lane.
howTheDrillWorks:
The transitioning team attempts to move possession through the corridor.
Central receivers lead into space and release before pressure closes.
Outside players hold width and remain available for release.
If the corridor remains open, the team may continue directly.
If defenders collapse centrally, the football is released to an outside lane.
One point is awarded for each controlled corridor possession.
Two points are awarded for breaking beyond the midfield line.
A bonus point is awarded when both outside lanes remain occupied.
Two additional points are awarded for reaching the scoring gate.
Defenders receive three points for forcing a central turnover.
Roles reverse immediately after a turnover.
Reset after a score, turnover or 40 seconds.
coachingPoints: Corridor players should receive while moving.
Outside players must resist following the football centrally.
The ball carrier should scan wide before central pressure arrives.
Width provides an escape and stretches the defence.
Support should remain behind as well as ahead of possession.
Central disposals must lead receivers away from pressure.
The team should avoid forcing corridor play when numbers close.
Players must transition defensively after a central turnover.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether central receivers scan before possession.
Quality of disposals through the corridor.
Whether safety support remains behind the football.
Defensive reaction after a central turnover.

commonErrors.error: Every player follows the football into the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain one option in each outside lane.

commonErrors.error: Central receivers stand still.
commonErrors.correction: Lead into the corridor as the previous player prepares to dispose.

commonErrors.error: The team forces the next central possession.
commonErrors.correction: Release wide when the corridor compresses.

commonErrors.error: Wide players become too disconnected.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust width so they remain within achievable disposal distance.

commonErrors.error: No player protects behind the central chain.
commonErrors.correction: Retain a trailing security player.

progressions: Add a recovering defender from behind.
Continue into a live forward entry.
Introduce scoreboard conditions that alter risk.
regressions: Reduce repeat running for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Release to outside space when required.
Prevent central turnovers from becoming direct scores.
matchApplication: Corridor transition can move the football quickly towards goal, but it becomes dangerous when every player compresses centrally. Maintaining outside width protects possession and preserves alternative routes.

title: False Corridor Entry
primarySkill: Using apparent corridor movement to create outside transition space.
objective: Develop coordinated movement that presents a credible corridor threat before releasing possession into outside space created by defensive compression.
groundSize: 75 metres long × 55 metres wide with a central corridor and two wide scoring lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central corridor approximately 15 metres wide.
Mark a wide scoring lane on each side.
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Position two central attacking receivers and wide players on both sides.
Begin with a defensive or midfield regain.
Position defenders to react strongly to central leads.
Retain at least one safety player behind the football.
howTheDrillWorks:
The transitioning team secures possession.
One or two central players lead visibly into the corridor.
The ball carrier presents as though the next disposal will travel centrally.
Defenders compress towards the corridor leads.
Wide players hold their lanes and prepare to receive.
The ball carrier releases to the side offering the greatest space.
One point is awarded when central movement draws defenders.
Two points are awarded for completing the wide release.
Two additional points are awarded for reaching a wide scoring gate.
Defenders receive three points for holding width and intercepting the release.
Roles reverse after a turnover.
Reset after a score, turnover or 40 seconds.
coachingPoints: The corridor movement must be credible enough to influence defenders.
Central players should not obstruct each other or become stationary targets.
Wide players must maintain width and timing.
The ball carrier should scan both sides before presenting centrally.
Release timing is critical once defenders compress.
Safety support must remain behind the initial movement.
The corridor may still be used when defenders fail to compress.
Players must avoid turning the pattern into a predetermined fake.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the central leads appear genuine.
Timing and direction of the release.
Whether the ball carrier scans both sides.
Whether the team uses the corridor when it remains available.
Whether defensive balance remains behind the football.

commonErrors.error: Central players make token movements that do not influence defenders.
commonErrors.correction: Lead with speed and present as genuine receiving options.

commonErrors.error: Wide players drift in before the release.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width until the defence commits centrally.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier decides the release side before scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Assess both wide lanes after defenders move.

commonErrors.error: The team refuses an open corridor because the drill expects width.
commonErrors.correction: Use the central option when defenders do not close it.

commonErrors.error: Security players follow the central leads.
commonErrors.correction: Remain connected behind possession.

progressions: Remove the corridor and lane markers.
Allow defenders to disguise whether they will compress.
Introduce a second wide release after the first is closed.
regressions: Give the transitioning team a numerical advantage.
Reduce the number of central receivers.
successIndicators: Retain the corridor when it remains open.
matchApplication: Teams can create outside transition space by presenting a genuine central threat. Defenders who compress towards the corridor may leave wide lanes available for fast release.
relatedDrills: TR-072 – Corridor Break and Hold Width

title: Midfield Unit Transition Roles
objective: Develop coordinated transition roles for inside midfielders, outside midfielders and defensive midfield support during repeated possession changes.
groundSize: Central 80 metres of the ground, including the centre square and both half-back and half-forward areas.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central playing area extending from half-back to half-forward.
Place a scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two midfield units.
Within each unit, identify:
Inside ball winner
Defensive midfielder
Forward-running midfielder
Outside midfielder
Underneath support midfielder
Begin from stoppages, loose footballs and coach-created turnovers.
Rotate roles every four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins with a midfield contest or controlled possession.
When a team gains possession, the inside ball winner secures and releases the football.
The outside midfielder provides width.
The forward-running midfielder moves ahead into attacking connection.
The underneath midfielder supports behind the football.
When possession is lost, the nearest midfielder pressures.
The defensive midfielder protects the corridor and tracks the most dangerous runner.
Other midfielders recover goal-side and reconnect with defenders.
The attacking team receives one point for exiting the contest and two points for reaching its scoring gate.
The defending team receives one point for forcing a backwards disposal and three for regaining possession.
Play continues through repeated turnovers for up to 45 seconds.
Reset and review role execution after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Inside midfielders must secure possession before releasing.
Outside midfielders should preserve width rather than entering every contest.
One midfielder should support underneath the football.
Forward runners must time movement to possession security.
The nearest player pressures after a turnover.
Defensive midfielders protect the corridor and dangerous runners.
Midfielders must work in both directions rather than specialising in one phase.
Communication should identify inside, outside, hold, recover and deepest roles.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether role clarity remains under fatigue.

commonErrors.error: Every midfielder attacks the initial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Hold one outside player and one underneath support player.

commonErrors.error: Forward runners leave before possession is secure.
commonErrors.correction: Time the run to the ball winner’s control.

commonErrors.error: No midfielder supports behind the football.
commonErrors.correction: Assign an underneath connection and security role.

commonErrors.error: Midfielders chase direct opponents into wide space.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the corridor and most dangerous runner first.

commonErrors.error: Players perform only attacking or defensive work.
commonErrors.correction: Rotate roles and score two-way transition actions.

progressions: Continue from midfield into full forward entries.
Require role handovers during the same phase.
regressions: Give the possession team a neutral midfielder.
Shorten repeated running for Over 35 players.
matchApplication: Midfielders are central to transition because they influence both the initial contest and the connection between defence and attack. Effective midfield units maintain role balance rather than sending every player towards the same action.

title: Wing Transition Roles
primarySkill: Executing wing-specific attacking and defensive transition roles.
objective: Develop wing players’ ability to provide attacking width, switch connection and defensive corridor support according to ball location and possession state.
groundSize: Approximately 80 metres long × 60 metres wide, using both wings and the corridor.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a near-side wing, corridor and far-side wing.
Place one scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams.
Assign one wing player to each side for both teams.
Position other players through half-back, midfield and half-forward.
Begin from defensive and midfield regains on alternating sides.
Rotate wing players every four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team gains possession near a boundary or through the corridor.
The near-side wing provides an immediate outside or forward option.
The far-side wing holds width and prepares for a switch.
If the team loses possession, the near-side wing pressures or tracks the outside outlet.
The far-side wing folds towards the corridor while preserving far-side awareness.
When possession changes again, both wings expand quickly.
One point is awarded for effective near-side support.
One point is awarded for maintaining usable far-side width.
Two points are awarded for a successful switch through a wing.
The defending team receives two points when a wing’s recovery closes a dangerous lane.
Play continues through repeated turnovers for 40 seconds.
Reset and alternate the starting side.
coachingPoints: Near-side and far-side wing roles differ.
The near-side wing should support the immediate possession phase.
The far-side wing must maintain width without becoming disconnected.
After losing possession, wings should fold enough to protect the corridor.
Wings must scan inside and behind, not only follow the boundary.
Far-side width can become the best attacking option after a regain.
Wing players should preserve the ability to move in both directions.
Communication should identify switch, fold, hold and inside support.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Position of near-side and far-side wings.
Whether wings fold appropriately in defence.
Whether wing receivers have inside support.
Whether players become trapped against the boundary.

commonErrors.error: Both wings move to the same side of the ground.
commonErrors.correction: Preserve far-side width and team balance.

commonErrors.error: The far-side wing remains too wide after possession is lost.
commonErrors.correction: Fold towards the corridor while tracking the switch threat.

commonErrors.error: The near-side wing stands flat-footed.
commonErrors.correction: Lead into space and provide a moving outlet.

commonErrors.error: Wings receive without inside support.
commonErrors.correction: Connect a midfielder or half-back beneath the wing.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after a switch disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Continue supporting the next forward action.

progressions: Require wing players to rotate with half-backs and half-forwards.
Continue into a full forward-entry phase.
regressions: Stop after each turnover to review wing positioning.
Reduce repeated running for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Execute different near-side and far-side roles.
matchApplication: Wing players provide critical balance during transition. Their positioning determines whether the team can access width in attack while still protecting the corridor and opposite-side movement in defence.
relatedDrills: TR-063 – Wing Release and Inside Support

title: Ruck and Stoppage Transition Roles
primarySkill: Executing ruck and stoppage-specific transition responsibilities.
objective: Develop coordinated transition roles for rucks, inside midfielders and outside stoppage players immediately after the stoppage outcome becomes clear.
groundSize: A 25-metre stoppage area inside a 65-metre × 45-metre transition field.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central stoppage circle or throw-in area.
Place a scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two stoppage units.
Within each unit, identify:
Ruck
First-possession midfielder
Defensive midfielder
Outside midfielder
High support player
Begin from ball-ups, boundary throw-ins and ground-ball stoppage simulations.
Rotate roles across several starts.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins the stoppage.
The rucks compete and follow the football after the hit-out.
Inside midfielders attempt to secure the first possession.
Outside players hold shape until the football’s direction becomes clear.
The team winning possession releases outside or forward.
The team losing possession pressures the clearance source.
The defensive midfielder protects the corridor and tracks the first forward runner.
The ruck either supports the clearance or folds behind the football.
One point is awarded for winning the first possession.
Two points are awarded for exiting the stoppage area under control.
Two additional points are awarded for reaching a scoring gate.
Reset after a score, turnover, secondary stoppage or 35 seconds.
coachingPoints: Rucks must transition after the hit-out rather than watching the outcome.
Inside midfielders should secure possession before forcing clearance.
Outside players must hold width and avoid collapsing early.
The team losing possession should pressure the source immediately.
Defensive midfielders protect the corridor and dangerous runners.
The ruck can become a support or defensive security player.
Players must react to the actual hit-out rather than the planned one.
Communication should identify possession, pressure, outside and recovery roles.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Ruck support behind or beside the football.

commonErrors.error: The ruck stops after the tap.
commonErrors.correction: Follow the football and become support or pressure.

commonErrors.error: Outside midfielders collapse into the stoppage.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width until possession direction is clear.

commonErrors.error: The clearance player kicks blindly.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession and use an outside or supported release.

commonErrors.error: Defensive midfielders chase the football.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the corridor and dangerous forward runner.

commonErrors.error: Players move according to the planned hit rather than the actual outcome.
commonErrors.correction: Read the live football and adjust immediately.

progressions: Introduce numerical imbalance outside the contest.
Add scoreboard and late-game stoppage scenarios.
Run consecutive stoppages without positional reset.
regressions: Give one team an extra outside player.
Reduce repeat efforts for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Follow the hit-out with a second action.
Use the ruck as support or security.
Transition from stoppage into open play.
matchApplication: Stoppages create immediate transition moments once possession becomes clear. Rucks and midfielders must move from set stoppage roles into open-play attack or defence without hesitation.

title: Kick-In to Open-Play Transition
primarySkill: Moving from a kick-in structure into open-play transition.
objective: Develop the team’s ability to launch from a kick-in, connect beyond defensive 50 and adapt when the planned exit becomes live open play.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use the goal square, defensive 50 and middle third.
Position one team in a kick-in structure.
Position the opposition in a zone, press or player-to-player structure.
Mark near-side, corridor and far-side exits beyond defensive 50.
Place target players through the middle third.
Prepare several opposition pressing structures.
Rotate kickers and primary outlet players.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins with a kick-in.
The kicker scans the opposition structure and selects an initial exit.
Defenders and midfielders move to create width, depth and switch support.
Once the first possession is completed, all kick-in restrictions end and play becomes live.
The team attempts to connect beyond defensive 50 and through the middle third.
If the planned option closes, the team uses a reset, switch or controlled contest.
One point is awarded for completing the first kick-in possession.
One point is awarded for exiting defensive 50.
Two points are awarded for controlled middle-third possession.
The opposition receives three points for scoring from a kick-in turnover.
Play continues for up to 45 seconds.
Reset from another kick-in using a different defensive press.
coachingPoints: The kick-in is the beginning of transition, not a separate isolated play.
Players should respond to the actual opposition structure.
The first receiver must have support for the next action.
Far-side options should remain available.
Players must not become fixed to the planned kick-in pattern.
Behind-ball security remains essential during the exit.
The kicker may become a supporting player after disposal.
The team must react defensively immediately if the kick-in turns over.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players remain fixed to a rehearsed pattern.

commonErrors.error: Players run predetermined routes despite opposition coverage.
commonErrors.correction: Read the live press and adapt the exit.

commonErrors.error: The first receiver is isolated.
commonErrors.correction: Build second and third actions around the initial kick.

commonErrors.error: Far-side players move towards the first option.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width and maintain switch potential.

commonErrors.error: The kicker stops after disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Become support behind or beside the football.

commonErrors.error: Players relax after exiting defensive 50.
commonErrors.correction: Continue transition through the middle third.

progressions: Allow the opposition to change its press during the kick-in.
Continue to a full-ground scoring phase.
Require players to identify the opposition structure before restarting.
regressions: Give the kick-in team an extra outlet player.
Reduce field length for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Adapt when the planned route closes.
matchApplication: A kick-in quickly becomes an open-play transition once the first possession is completed. Successful teams connect their starting structure to the next several actions rather than judging success only by the first kick.
relatedDrills: TR-009 – First Exit After Defensive Regain

title: Match Scenario Transition Simulation
primarySkill: Applying complete transition systems across realistic match scenarios.
objective: Prepare players for the final chapter assessment by integrating position-specific roles, turnover-zone responses, match context and full-ground transition under realistic pressure.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use the full oval.
Divide players into two balanced match teams.
Establish normal positional structures.
Prepare six scenarios:
Defensive 50 regain against a high press
Midfield turnover with numerical advantage
Midfield turnover while outnumbered
Forward-half regain
Kick-in transition
Red-time scoreboard transition
Assign coaching observers to defence, midfield, wings and forwards.
Player leaders manage communication and structure.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins Scenario 1 and allows play to continue until the objective is completed or possession stabilises.
The next scenario starts immediately from a different field position.
Players must reorganise without a complete positional reset.
Position groups execute their transition responsibilities.
Normal match scoring applies.
One team-structure point is awarded for maintaining line connection.
One decision-quality point is awarded for selecting an appropriate transition response.
One defensive point is awarded for organised pressure and recovery after losing possession.
An avoidable turnover caused by poor transition balance removes one point.
Complete the six-scenario sequence twice.
On the second sequence, alter opposition tactics and scoreboard conditions.
Finish with five minutes of unrestricted play.
coachingPoints: Position-specific roles must support the whole-team response.
Players should recognise field position before selecting transition speed.
Numerical advantage should be used before it disappears.
Numerical disadvantage should be managed through security and delay.
Defensive 50 regains require calm exit connection.
Forward-half regains require organised scoring and pressure.
Kick-in structure must flow into open play.
Red-time scenarios alter risk and tempo.
Leadership communication should organise without removing player decision making.
Transition behaviours must remain during unrestricted play.

commonErrors.error: Position groups perform their roles without connecting to teammates.
commonErrors.correction: Judge every role by its effect on the complete team structure.

commonErrors.error: Players wait for a full reset between scenarios.
commonErrors.correction: Reorganise immediately from the current field position.

commonErrors.error: The same transition route is used repeatedly.
commonErrors.correction: Read pressure, field position and available numbers.

commonErrors.error: Leaders give constant instructions that slow decisions.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate essential information and allow teammates to act.

commonErrors.error: Structure disappears during unrestricted play.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce the same principles without drill scoring or coach prompts.

progressions: Allow opposition teams to create their own scenarios.
Use video and GPS data where available.
Include special situations such as a player off the ground or deliberate defensive spare.
regressions: Shorten the simulation for Over 35 players.
matchApplication: This simulation combines the position-specific, tactical and contextual demands of transition. It tests whether the team can move between different match situations without relying on complete resets or constant coach direction.

title: Transition Chapter Final Assessment
primarySkill: Demonstrating complete individual, positional and team transition capability.
objective: Complete the final assessment of the Transition chapter by evaluating whether players and the team can independently recognise, organise and execute all major transition behaviours under full match conditions.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use the full oval.
Divide players into two balanced match teams.
Use normal positional structures and rotations.
Assign observers to assess:
Individual transition reaction
Defensive unit
Midfield unit
Wings
Forward unit
Whole-team shape
Match-context decision making
Prepare assessment categories covering the full chapter:
Turnover recognition
First-three-second response
Immediate pressure
Corridor recovery
First-possession security
Attacking spread
Support running
Defensive exit
Team line connection
Position-specific roles
Numerical decision making
Scoreboard management
Turnover protection
Communication and leadership
Begin with normal match conditions rather than a predetermined pattern.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins as a full match simulation.
Coaches allow natural turnovers to occur without immediate intervention.
During the first block, no bonus points or coach prompts are used.
During the second block, the coach introduces selected scenarios including:
Defensive 50 regain
Central turnover
Forward-half regain
Stoppage spill
Kick-in
Numerical imbalance
Red-time scoreboard situation
Normal match scoring applies throughout.
Individual players are assessed on recognition, effort, role execution and decision quality.
Position groups are assessed on connection and role clarity.
The whole team is assessed on shape change, route selection and turnover protection.
Play four blocks of eight to ten minutes.
Give only brief principle-based feedback between blocks.
Complete the final block without coach-created scenarios or transition scoring.
Conduct a post-session review using observations, player feedback and video where available.
coachingPoints: Players must recognise turnovers independently.
The first three seconds should contain purposeful attacking or defensive action.
Nearest-player pressure must be supported by cover and balance.
Defensive recovery should protect corridor, goal-side and deepest space.
Regains must be secured through the first and second possessions.
The attacking team should create width, depth and connected support.
Defensive exits require composure and several linked actions.
Team lines must move together through full-ground transition.
Position-specific responsibilities must contribute to the complete team shape.
Numerical advantage and disadvantage must be recognised quickly.
Scoreboard, time and field position should influence risk.
High-risk transition requires protection behind the football.
Communication must be early, specific and useful.
Transition behaviours should remain without external scoring or coach prompts.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Security of the first two possessions.
Connection between defenders, midfielders, wings and forwards.

commonErrors.error: Players recognise turnovers only after teammates react.
commonErrors.correction: Scan continuously and take independent responsibility for the first action.

commonErrors.error: Pressure is applied without support behind it.
commonErrors.correction: Establish cover, corridor protection and deeper balance.

commonErrors.error: The team wins possession but loses the next disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the first and second possessions before expanding fully.

commonErrors.error: Position groups become disconnected.
commonErrors.correction: Move the entire team shape with the football.

commonErrors.error: Players use the same transition response in every location.
commonErrors.correction: Match the action to field position, pressure, numbers and scoreboard.

commonErrors.error: Aggressive transition leaves no protection behind.
commonErrors.correction: Organise security before attempting high-risk movement.

commonErrors.error: Communication disappears under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain clear role and pressure calls throughout the session.

commonErrors.error: Behaviours appear only during coach-created scenarios.
commonErrors.correction: Assess and reinforce transition habits during unrestricted play.

progressions: Extend into full quarter-length match simulation.
Use full senior match contact where appropriate.
Allow teams to design and alter their own transition systems.
Include opposition tactical changes between quarters.
Add player-number scenarios such as rotations, injuries or temporary imbalance.
Use detailed video coding and statistical transition review.
Establish individual and positional development plans from assessment results.
regressions: Assess one half of the ground at a time.
Reduce player numbers and field dimensions.
Evaluate selected transition categories rather than the full chapter.
Pause after major turnovers to review shape.
Shorten blocks and running distances for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Apply organised pressure and defensive recovery.
Secure the first and second possessions.
Create attacking width, depth and support.
Sustain repeat effort and decision quality.
Reproduce transition behaviours during unrestricted match play.
matchApplication: This final assessment represents the complete Transition chapter. It determines whether players can independently move from attack to defence and defence to attack across contests, field positions, positional roles, tactical systems and match scenarios. Successful performance indicates that transition principles have become repeatable team behaviours rather than isolated drill actions.
relatedDrills: TR-070 – Team Ball Movement Transition Assessment

title: Football Movement Preparation Flow
